question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to casualty 45 minutes after ingesting approximately 20 mL of kerosene from a soft-drink bottle stored in the kitchen. He is alert, has mild coughing, and smells of kerosene. His oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step in management?

answers.text: Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally to reduce systemic absorption

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Activated charcoal is ineffective for hydrocarbon ingestion because kerosene is not well-adsorbed by charcoal, and its administration risks vomiting and subsequent aspiration — which is the primary danger in kerosene ingestion.

answers.text: Provide supportive care with close monitoring of respiratory status and avoid inducing vomiting or gastric lavage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Management of kerosene ingestion is entirely supportive. Emesis and gastric lavage are absolutely contraindicated because they dramatically increase the risk of aspiration of the low-viscosity hydrocarbon into the lungs, which is the principal cause of morbidity and mortality.

answers.text: Perform gastric lavage with a cuffed endotracheal tube in situ to remove the kerosene

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gastric lavage is contraindicated in kerosene ingestion even when a cuffed ETT is in place. The risk of aspiration during lavage outweighs any benefit, as the amount absorbed systemically is small and kerosene toxicity is predominantly from aspiration, not systemic ingestion.

answers.text: Administer syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting and expel the ingested kerosene

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Inducing vomiting with ipecac or any other method is absolutely contraindicated in kerosene ingestion. Vomiting forces the volatile low-viscosity hydrocarbon to contact the laryngopharynx, vastly increasing aspiration risk and potentially causing a chemical pneumonitis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: emesis and lavage are absolutely contraindicated in kerosene ingestion because aspiration — not systemic absorption — is the primary threat. Management is supportive.

Excellent. The cardinal rule of kerosene management is: do NOT induce vomiting, do NOT perform gastric lavage, do NOT give activated charcoal. Supportive care and respiratory monitoring are the mainstay of treatment.
